extracted.intended_audience: high-school and undergraduate students preparing for trigonometry contests/ olympiads and instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques, identities, and solution strategies for a wide range of contest-style trigonometry problems (identities, inequalities, triangle geometry, and algebraic manipulations), as presented in a problem-and-solution textbook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of double-angle and half-angle formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent application of double-angle and half-angle identities (e.g., cos 3x = 4 cos^3 x − 3 cos x; 4 cos^2 x − 3 = cos 3x; sin x cos x = (1/2) sin 2x; 1 − cos x = 2 sin^2(x/2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transform expressions involving multiples or halves of angles to simpler trigonometric forms; used to reduce products/powers or evaluate expressions (Problems 16, 22, 25, 26, 34).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum-to-product and product-to-sum transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply sum-to-product and product-to-sum formulas to rewrite sums of sines/cosines as products and vice versa (e.g., sin u + sin v = 2 sin[(u+v)/2] cos[(u−v)/2]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for simplifying cyclic sums, proving identities like sin 2A + sin 2B + sin 2C = 4 sin A sin B sin C, and for converting sums into factorable products (Problems 15, 24, 27, 38).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of addition and subtraction formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Use addition/subtraction identities (sin(α±β), cos(α±β), tan(α±β)) to combine or split angle expressions and to recognize tan(2a + a) = tan 3a, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key for proving angle-sum identities and for algebraic manipulation that shows one trigonometric expression equals another (Problems 13, 19, 20, 29, many solutions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairing factors using complementary or symmetric angles
rubrics_metrics.description: Pair terms like (1 + tan k°) and (1 + tan(45° − k°)) to produce simple constants (e.g., product equals 2), or pair sin/cos factors symmetrically to telescope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A combinatorial/product trick for evaluating large products by grouping complementary indices (Problem 30).

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic substitution (tan, sin, cos substitutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make substitutions such as a = tan x, x1 = c cos θ, or sin(A/2) = x to convert trigonometric statements into algebraic ones or to parameterize points on circles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use substitutions to translate trig conditions into polynomial/quadratic equations or to parametrize geometric constraints (Problems 36, 42, 45).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the law of sines, law of cosines, and extended law of sines
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply law of sines/cosines and R = a/(2 sin A) and relations like r(|AB|+|BC|+|CA|) = 2([AI B]+[BI C]+[CI A]) to relate side lengths, angles, circumradius R, inradius r, and areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential for triangle geometry problems connecting side ratios, areas, and circle radii; used to derive formulas (Problems 25, 26, 31, 33).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometry via similarity and homothety (incenters/inradii)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use homothety/similarity arguments that relate an inner triangle (e.g., triangle E F G) to the reference triangle ABC via the incenter and inradius (r and r−1), yielding scale ratios and proportional side/area relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when triangles are parallel or homothetic (incenter as center) to compute lengths or area ratios (Problem 1/first solutions sketch at top of chunk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigonometric Ceva and concurrency criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the trigonometric form of Ceva's theorem: product of (sin of directed angle ratios) = 1 to prove concurrency of cevians (e.g., show AG, BD, CE are concurrent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use in triangle geometry when proving lines meet at a point (Problem 50).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of classical inequalities (AM–GM and Cauchy–Schwarz)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply arithmetic–geometric mean inequality and Cauchy–Schwarz to derive bounds and minima/maxima for expressions involving trig functions and to compare sums/products (used repeatedly: AM–GM, Cauchy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard tool for establishing inequalities involving sums/products of sines, cosines, tangents (Problems 17, 19(b), 20(b), 23, 28, 39, 43, 46).

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert trig inequalities to algebraic ones via monotonicity or boundedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit ranges of trig functions (e.g., sin x cos x ≤ 1/2) to bound expressions and reduce inequalities to solvable algebraic constraints (Problem 17, 40).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sin x cos x has a maximum, use it to bound related expressions and solve for variables (Problem 17 & 40 approach).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of induction (including strong induction) for sequence/polynomial properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply (strong) induction to prove properties of recursively defined polynomials or sequences (e.g., Chebyshev polynomials: Tn+1 = 2xTn − Tn−1 and Tn(cos θ) = cos(nθ)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induction is used to prove parity (odd/even), monotonicity for x>1, and the identity Tn(cos θ) = cos(nθ) (Problem 49).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameterization of geometric loci
rubrics_metrics.description: Parametrize points on circles/curves (e.g., x1 = c cos θ, x2 = c sin θ) to convert constrained optimization or coordinate geometry problems into trigonometric expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful to transform problems about points on a circle into problems about angles that can be optimized or simplified (Problem 42).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairing/tracking signs and absolute values with triangle/angle constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: When dealing with absolute values or sign-dependent trig sums, use triangle-angle relationships and induction to compare |sin ai| + |cos(sum)| terms and deduce lower bounds (Problem 47).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handle absolute values carefully; reduce multi-term inequalities by stepwise comparison of partial sums and using trig addition formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of classical area and perimeter relations (Heron, s, r, R identities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Heron's formula and well-known relations: [ABC] = rs, R = abc/(4[ABC]), sin(A/2) formula in terms of semiperimeter to derive identities connecting r, R, s, and side lengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply to deduce formulas for r and R and to prove inequalities involving s and R (Problems 25, 26, 27).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit symmetry and reorderings to simplify expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reorder symmetric sums or group symmetric terms to apply inequalities or identities more easily (e.g., sum cyclic sin^2(A/2) bounds, symmetric use in Problem 28).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize symmetric structure to apply AM–GM, Cauchy, or to reduce to known symmetric inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of complex/trigonometric product manipulations to evaluate large products
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate large cosine/sine products by expressing them as products of 2 sin x cos x factors and using periodicity/paired terms to collapse the product (Problem 38 approach: P and Q trick).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce auxiliary products (e.g., Q = sin a sin 2a ... ) and show relationships like (2 sin x cos x) across index ranges to deduce closed forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and use special angles and constructions (Brocard point, altitudes, special angle measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce classical geometric points (Brocard point) or construct altitudes and midpoints to exploit known angle measures or concurrence properties in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use known special points/angles when the problem hints at cyclic symmetry or when bounding angles (Problem 51, Problem 50).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of root-location and orthogonality arguments for polynomial/trigonometric equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine roots of polynomials like Chebyshev polynomials Tn(x) by mapping x = cos θ and using Tn(cos θ) = cos(nθ) to locate roots in [−1,1].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transform polynomial root problems into angle equations (nθ = (2k+1)π/2), yielding explicit root sets (Problem 49(d),(e)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform product-sum/triple-angle identities into tangent relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Show identities involving tangent sums/products by algebraic manipulation of tan addition formulas (e.g., derive tan 3a relation and generalization tan a1 + tan a2 + tan a3 = tan a1 tan a2 tan a3 when a1+a2+a3=0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tangent addition formula to transform complicated sums into the standard tan( sum ) form and thereby prove equalities (Problems 13 and note after).
